intro:
These exercises rehearse the one discipline the chapter is built around: before rewriting any function, split a slow request's wall time into the layers it actually spends time in, point at the widest layer, and only then confirm with a sampler or trace. Every problem here is a small, runnable version of that move. The data structures are deliberately tiny so the result stays easy to trace, but the logic is the same one a flame graph performs for you visually.

You will start by matching profiling questions to the instrument that answers each with the least distortion, then implement the per-stage and per-layer reductions, isolate fixed per-crossing overhead at a WASM/FFI boundary, separate the two halves of lock cost, and finally write the decompose-first plan that settles a cross-team p99 dispute. The connecting thread is that a profiler narrows a judgment; it never removes one. Choosing the wrong build, the wrong workload, or the wrong metric still sends a senior team at the wrong fix.

exerciseSolutions.title: Match the question to the instrument
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The chapter's core rule is that the toolkit fans out from one decision: what kind of answer do you need? Walk the decision diagram from the question, not from the tool you happen to have open. Each of the three questions points at a different instrument, and reaching for the wrong one distorts the answer rather than failing loudly.

"Is version B actually faster than version A under a fixed workload?" is a comparison question, so the instrument is a benchmark, and Criterion is the ecosystem default. It runs the measured closure many times, discards warmup, and reports a distribution with confidence intervals rather than a single number, so it can tell you which alternative won and by how much without you eyeballing a stopwatch. A CPU sampler is the wrong first tool here because a sampler explains where compute concentrates inside one binary; it does not compare two implementations and will not tell you whether the difference between A and B is real or noise.

"Where is compute time concentrating in this running binary?" is a localization question, so the instrument is a sampling CPU profiler. It interrupts the running binary many times per second, records the call stack, and aggregates those samples into a statistical picture of where compute time concentrates, perturbing the program very little. A benchmark is the wrong tool here because it compares, it does not explain: it can tell you A is slower than B but not which stack inside A owns the time.

A CPU sampler is the wrong first instrument for an async task that takes 200ms of wall time but almost no CPU because a sampler only sees code that runs often enough to be caught between samples. The 200ms was spent enqueued, waiting on a semaphore permit, or parked on the blocking thread pool, and none of that is executing instructions the sampler can catch, so the profile comes back nearly empty and points at nothing. The right signal for a wall-time gap is tracing spans around each transition, which record where the task actually waits or blocks rather than where it burns cores.
criteria: Names Criterion for the version-versus-version benchmark and a sampling CPU profiler for locating the hot compute path.
Explains that a sampler only captures code that runs often enough to be hit between samples, so it misses time spent enqueued, awaiting a permit, or parked.
States that an async wall-time gap is diagnosed with tracing spans around each transition, not with CPU samples.
Justifies each instrument by the question being asked rather than by whichever tool is already open.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the hottest-stage reduction
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The function is hottest_stage(samples: &[StageSample]) -> (&'static str, u64, u64), and it performs two reductions over the same slice. The sample data is parse=180, serialize=620, lock_wait=40.

The line let total: u64 = samples.iter().map(|sample| sample.micros).sum() borrows each StageSample, projects out its micros field, and folds the stream with addition. On the sample data this is 180 + 620 + 40 = 840 microseconds, the wall time spent across all stages.

The expression samples.iter().max_by_key(|sample| sample.micros) scans the slice and returns the StageSample with the largest micros value, wrapped in Some because the iterator yields elements. For this input that is serialize at 620. The .copied() turns the &StageSample into an owned StageSample, which is cheap because StageSample derives Copy, and .unwrap() is safe here because the slice is non-empty, so max_by_key cannot return None and unwrap cannot panic on this input.

The function returns the tuple (hottest.name, hottest.micros, total), which evaluates to ("serialize", 620, 840) in name, hottest-micros, total order. This max-over-stages reduction is the same question a flame graph answers visually: reducing a list of timings to one named winner is exactly what the flame graph does when it points you at the widest stack. The widest box owns the most aggregate sampled time, and serialize at 620 of 840 is the widest box in this data.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Hand-traced: the two reductions yield total 840 and hottest serialize at 620, returning ("serialize", 620, 840).
criteria: The total is computed as 180 + 620 + 40 = 840 microseconds and identified as the sum of all stage micros.
max_by_key is identified as selecting the StageSample with the largest micros, returning serialize at 620.
The returned tuple is given as ("serialize", 620, 840) in name, hottest-micros, total order.
The answer connects reducing a list of timings to one named winner with the flame graph pointing at the widest stack.

exerciseSolutions.title: Report each stage as a share of wall time
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The goal is to turn the per-stage decomposition into a percentage breakdown so the widest layer is obvious before any tuning begins. The signature is fn share_of_total(samples: &[StageSample]) -> Vec<(&'static str, u64)>, taking a shared slice so the caller keeps ownership of its Vec and the function only needs read access.

Compute the total once with a single pass, then map each sample to (name, sample.micros * 100 / total). The order of operations matters: multiply by 100 before dividing by total so the fraction survives integer truncation. For parse=180 the correct path is 180 * 100 / 840 = 18000 / 840 = 21 (truncated); dividing first would compute 180 / 840 = 0 and then 0 * 100 = 0, collapsing every small stage to zero. With this ordering the result for parse=180, serialize=620, lock_wait=40 is [("parse", 21), ("serialize", 73), ("lock_wait", 4)]. Note that integer truncation means these shares sum to 98, not 100; that is expected, so do not assert that the breakdown adds up to exactly 100.

The empty-slice case must be handled before any division, because total would be zero and micros * 100 / 0 would panic. I return an empty Vec for an empty input: there are no stages to report a share of, so the natural answer is the empty breakdown. Guarding on samples.is_empty() (or, equivalently, on total == 0) keeps the divide-by-zero from ever executing. Everything else is integer arithmetic with no per-stage allocation beyond the result Vec itself.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Two-pass integer reduction: sum once, then map each stage to micros * 100 / total, with an empty-slice guard.
criteria: The signature is exactly fn share_of_total(samples: &[StageSample]) -> Vec<(&'static str, u64)>.
For parse=180, serialize=620, lock_wait=40 the result is [("parse", 21), ("serialize", 73), ("lock_wait", 4)].
Percentages use micros * 100 / total with multiplication before division, preserving the truncated fraction.
The empty-slice case returns an empty Vec, guarding before any division so total == 0 never divides.

exerciseSolutions.title: Measure fixed per-crossing overhead
exerciseSolutions.solution:
WASM and FFI share one failure mode: the cost is rarely in the Rust kernel and almost always in the crossing. The single highest-leverage experiment for both is to compare a noop call (tiny or empty payload) against the real call. The noop isolates the marshalling and call cost, so the difference between them is the fixed per-crossing overhead rather than the work of the callee or the kernel.

The signature is fn crossing_overhead(noop_ns: u64, real_ns: u64, calls: u64) -> (u64, u64), returning (per_call_overhead_ns, total_overhead_ns). Per-call overhead is real_ns minus noop_ns, but the subtraction must use saturating_sub. A noisy noop measurement can land above the real call, and unguarded u64 subtraction wraps on underflow, producing an absurd near-u64::MAX number; saturating_sub clamps that case to 0 instead. Total overhead is the per-call overhead multiplied by calls.

For noop_ns=30, real_ns=110, calls=1_000_000 the per-call overhead is 110 saturating_sub 30 = 80 ns, and the total is 80 * 1_000_000 = 80_000_000 ns. The reason this number drives an API decision is that a large per-crossing overhead is paid on every single call regardless of how fast the callee is. When the fixed cost dominates, a batched API that crosses the boundary once will beat any amount of tuning on the callee, because tuning the kernel cannot touch the part of the cost that lives in the crossing itself.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: noop subtracted from real call via saturating_sub isolates per-crossing overhead; scaled by call count for the total.
criteria: The signature is exactly fn crossing_overhead(noop_ns: u64, real_ns: u64, calls: u64) -> (u64, u64).
For noop_ns=30, real_ns=110, calls=1_000_000 it returns (80, 80_000_000).
The subtraction uses saturating_sub, so noop_ns greater than real_ns yields 0 rather than wrapping.
A comment states that high fixed overhead favors crossing once with a batch over tuning the callee.

exerciseSolutions.title: Fix a lock metric that hides contention
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that a single lock_cost_us conflates the two halves of lock cost the chapter insists on separating. The teammate's number is hold time only: the time a thread spends holding the guard and doing work. Wait time, the time other threads spend blocked waiting to acquire the lock, is never recorded. The two halves fail in opposite ways, so collapsing them into one averaged number erases exactly the signal needed to spot contention. The conclusion that a hot lock is fine because its number is small is therefore unjustified, because the small number is hold time and the missing number is wait time.

The fix is to replace the single field with a struct that stores hold_us and wait_us separately and reports both. classify(hold_us, wait_us) -> &'static str then returns "contention" when wait_us exceeds hold_us and "hold" otherwise. For (hold_us=5, wait_us=900) it returns "contention"; for (hold_us=900, wait_us=5) it returns "hold".

A lock held briefly but acquired constantly shows exactly this contention shape: low hold_us, high wait_us. Each critical section is short, so the guard is held only momentarily and hold_us stays small, but the lock is acquired so frequently that threads pile up waiting their turn, and that queue is where the wall time goes. A single averaged number would hide this because the brief hold time would dominate the average and make the lock look cheap.

Before reaching for lower-level lock-free structures, the chapter says to try the cheaper redesigns first, because a hot lock is often an ownership problem hiding underneath rather than only a synchronization one. Narrow the shared state so fewer threads contend for the same lock, shorten the critical section so the guard is held for less time, shard the state so contention spreads across several locks, move to a read-mostly design when writes are rare, or give a subsystem its own owner so its state is not shared at all. Reach for lock-free structures last, after those redesigns have been tried.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: hold_us and wait_us are stored separately; classify names the dominant half instead of averaging the two away.
criteria: Hold time and wait time are stored and reported as two separate fields rather than one combined number.
classify returns "contention" for (5, 900) and "hold" for (900, 5).
The explanation ties high wait_us with low hold_us to a frequently-acquired short critical section.
The answer names narrowing shared state, shortening critical sections, sharding, or giving a subsystem its own owner (read-mostly redesign included) before going lock-free.

exerciseSolutions.title: Resolve the p99 regression argument
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The argument cannot be settled by any of the three signals on its own, because each engineer is reading one layer of a request that lives in several. The plan is to decompose one slow request's wall time into its layers before any function is rewritten, point at the widest layer, and only then confirm the call stack. Optimizing on sight is the failure mode this discipline exists to prevent.

The layers and their instruments are: CPU compute, measured with a sampling CPU profiler; queue wait, measured with tracing spans around the enqueue-to-dequeue transition; lock blocking, measured by recording hold time and wait time separately per lock; IO, measured with a trace that captures time queued before the IO begins, not CPU samples; serialization, measured by encode and decode time alongside allocations per message and bytes per message; and boundary-crossing overhead, measured by comparing a noop crossing against the real one. Each engineer's signal becomes one named layer with a budget rather than the whole story.

The order of operations is fixed: decompose the wall time into those layers first, point at the widest layer, then confirm the call stack with a sampler or trace. The widest stage is only the first suspect, not the verdict. The chief guard against blaming the first recognizable function is that a wide serialize stack is frequently the allocation and copy beneath it rather than the encoder's control flow, so tuning the serializer would barely move the number while cutting the copy would. The same guard applies to IO: a sampler shows the CPU busy inside a parser and the parser gets blamed, while a trace reveals the request spent most of its life queued before the parser ever ran. So the rule is to confirm what sits beneath the wide box before touching it.

The discipline I will hold the team to is one bounded question, one build, and one recorded workload. The question is scoped to a single thing such as "which layer owns the p99 wall-time increase since the release," not "make it faster." The build is one release build with symbols good enough for usable stacks, because a debug build profiles a different program. The workload is one recorded, representative input replayed identically, so that the engineer who later has to reproduce the regression measures the same thing the person who captured it did. One question, one build, one recorded workload keeps the profile an answer instead of a new argument.
criteria: The plan enumerates CPU compute, queue wait, lock blocking, IO, serialization, and boundary-crossing overhead, each paired with a fitting instrument.
The sequence is decompose first, point at the widest layer, then confirm the call stack with a sampler or trace, not optimize-on-sight.
The plan warns a wide serialize stack may be the allocation and copy beneath it, and an IO path's real cost is often queue time, not CPU samples.
Scope is fixed to one bounded question, one release build with usable symbols, and one recorded representative workload.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
dominant = cpu
wall us = 800
dominant share = 51
labSolution.explanation:
The lab decomposes a pipeline's wall time into four named layers and then names the layer that owns the most time, which is the core move of the whole chapter expressed in a few runnable lines. The layers function projects the PipelineStats fields into a fixed array of (name, micros) pairs, and wall_time folds that array with sum to get the total: 410 + 120 + 90 + 180 = 800 microseconds.

The only piece to fill in is dominant. It calls layers(stats).into_iter() to take the array by value (so each tuple is owned, not borrowed), then max_by_key(|(_, value)| *value) selects the pair with the largest micros, and unwrap is safe because the array always has four elements and can never be empty. For this data the largest is ("cpu", 410), so dominant returns that pair.

In main the share is computed as micros * 100 / wall = 410 * 100 / 800 = 41000 / 800, where integer division truncates 51.25 to 51, multiplying before dividing so the fraction is not lost. The program therefore prints dominant = cpu, wall us = 800, and dominant share = 51, which matches the expected output exactly. The reduction from a list of timings to one named winner is the same question a flame graph answers by pointing at the widest stack.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does choosing a profiling instrument start from the question you need answered rather than from the tool you already have open?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because each instrument answers one kind of question and distorts the others: a benchmark compares two implementations but does not explain why one won, a sampler localizes hot compute but cannot compare versions, and a trace shows where time is spent waiting but is not a CPU picture. If you start from whatever tool is already open, you bend the question to fit the tool and get a confident answer to the wrong question. The chapter's rule is to walk the decision diagram from the question to the instrument that answers it with the least distortion.

reviewAnswers.question: What does the x-axis of a flame graph represent, and why is reading it as a timeline a mistake?
reviewAnswers.answer: The x-axis is not chronological time; it groups boxes by the shape of the call stack, and the width of each box is the total sampled time attributed to that stack. The stack grows upward, so a wide box means that stack owned a lot of aggregate sampled time, not that it ran at a particular moment. Reading it left-to-right as a timeline leads you to infer an order of execution that the graph never encoded, and to miss that width, not horizontal position, is the signal that points at the widest stack.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the tradeoff between sampling and instrumentation, and when does each one mislead you?
reviewAnswers.answer: Sampling watches from the outside at a fixed rate, so it perturbs the program very little but only sees code that runs often enough to be caught between samples; it misleads you by missing rare-but-expensive paths and time spent waiting, parked, or enqueued, which execute no instructions to catch. Instrumentation records explicit measurements at chosen points, so it is precise about exactly those points but adds overhead and can perturb the very thing it measures, especially in hot loops where the instrumentation cost rivals the work. The choice is overhead versus precision: use sampling to find where compute concentrates cheaply, and instrumentation when you need an exact number for a specific transition.

reviewAnswers.question: Why can a CPU profiler tell only part of the story for an async task that takes 200ms of wall time but almost no CPU?
reviewAnswers.answer: A CPU profiler only sees instructions executing on a core, but most of those 200ms were spent enqueued, waiting on a semaphore permit, or parked on the blocking thread pool, where the task is not running any code to sample. The profile comes back nearly empty and points at nothing, because the wall-time gap lives in waiting, not in compute. The right signal is tracing spans around each transition, which record where the task actually waits or blocks; the fix usually lives in admission policy or queue wait, almost never in rewriting the executor.

reviewAnswers.question: What are the two halves of lock cost that must be measured separately, and how does each one fail differently?
reviewAnswers.answer: The two halves are hold time, the time a thread spends holding the guard doing work, and wait time, the time other threads spend blocked waiting to acquire the lock. They fail in opposite ways: a lock held briefly but acquired constantly shows low hold time yet high wait time and is a contention problem, while a lock held for a long stretch shows high hold time and is a critical-section-length problem. Collapsing them into one averaged number erases exactly the signal you need, and because a hot lock is often an ownership problem underneath, the cheaper fixes are to narrow shared state, shorten critical sections, or give a subsystem its own owner before reaching for lock-free structures.
